name: Betaine

lead: Betaine (trimethylglycine) is a compound found in beets, spinach, wheat and shellfish, and sold as a pre-workout supplement. Lifters take it for more strength and power and a fuller, better-hydrated muscle look.

It acts as an osmolyte that protects cells under stress and as a methyl donor, and proponents link it to cell hydration, creatine synthesis and anabolic signalling. A meta-analysis found a small gain in maximal strength, mainly lower body, while results for body composition and power are mixed across small, short trials.

paras: Taken as a powder or capsule, often inside pre-workout blends, on training days or daily alongside other staples such as creatine. Trials have run for a few weeks, and users judge it by how heavy and how many reps they can handle over a training block.

Legal and low in acute toxicity. Stomach upset and a fishy odor can occur, and it may raise cholesterol in some people. A prescription form exists for homocystinuria, and betaine hydrochloride sold for digestion is a different product.

angle.text: Users take betaine as a training supplement to get more strength and power, which feeds harder, heavier sessions and a fuller, leaner muscle look. Small trials have measured strength and body composition with mixed results. Claims about cortisol and overtraining come mostly from limited or anecdotal reports.

lead: Betaine, also called trimethylglycine (TMG) or glycine betaine, is a small N-trimethylated amino acid derivative first isolated from sugar beets, after which it is named [1][2]. It occurs in beets, spinach, quinoa, wheat and seafood, is made in the body from choline, and acts both as a methyl donor in one-carbon metabolism and as an osmolyte that protects cells and enzymes under stress [1][2][3].

For appearance, betaine anhydrous is taken as a sports supplement by lifters aiming at a better physique: more strength and power for training, support for lean mass and a leaner body composition. It appears in pre-workout powders and is marketed with claims about cell hydration, cortisol and recovery [4][5][6][7].

Human trials on exercise performance are small and short. A 2024 meta-analysis of 17 studies reported higher maximal strength with betaine, especially in the lower body, while a 2022 meta-analysis found no significant change in body composition measures [8][9]. Individual trials in CrossFit athletes, cyclists and footballers have reported mixed results [10][11][12][13]. A separate pharmaceutical betaine is prescribed for homocystinuria [2]. The term 'betaine' also covers a chemical class, and betaine hydrochloride sold for digestion is a different product [1].

paras: Betaine anhydrous is taken for strength and power training and sometimes for body composition. T Nation's pre-workout products list 2 to 2.5 g servings alongside citrulline malate and beta-alanine [4][5][6][14]. The site's descriptions say betaine promotes intracellular hydration and cell volumisation and reduces cortisol to mitigate overtraining stress [6][7]. Forum users list it among pre-workout ingredients in training logs [15].

Trials in athletes usually give betaine as a powder in a drink or capsules for one to several weeks and measure squat and bench performance, jump height, sprint power, hormone levels and body composition [16][10][12][13][17].

Betaine is a prescription medicine for homocystinuria, a genetic disorder of methionine metabolism, according to Grokipedia [2]. A registered trial studied betaine metabolism in homocystinuria (NCT02404337) [18]. Other trials have examined betaine in peroxisome biogenesis disorders, steatohepatitis, lipid metabolism in overweight women and in lactating mothers [19][20][21][22][23]. Cosmetic products use betaine as a humectant and skin conditioner, and cocamidopropyl betaine derivatives are surfactants in shampoos [1][2].

Studies of betaine and exercise are mixed and mostly short. Reviews describe both positive and null results across strength, power and body-composition outcomes [24][25]. Details are given under Clinical studies.

Strength and power. A 2010 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial by Lee and colleagues at the University of Connecticut gave 12 resistance-trained men betaine in a sports drink for two 14-day periods. Isometric bench press and squat force and bench throw power were higher with betaine, repetitions to fatigue did not differ, and the study was funded by a betaine manufacturer with a company co-author [16]. The authors noted that an earlier study by Hoffman and colleagues found no differences in bench press, vertical jump or Wingate performance, with more squat repetitions on some days [16].

A 2017 systematic review by Ismaeel of seven randomized trials rated 'excellent' on the PEDro scale reported that two found increases in strength or power and five found no change [24]. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis by Zawieja and colleagues in the Journal of Sports Sciences pooled 17 studies with 317 participants. It reported a standardized mean difference of 0.47 for maximal strength, 0.49 for lower-body strength and 0.36 for vertical jump (after excluding one low-quality study), with no significant effects on upper-body strength, cycling sprint power, bench throw power or muscular endurance, and concluded that supplementation of at least seven days enhances strength [8].

Body composition. A 2022 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Nutrition by Ashtary-Larky and colleagues, covering studies to August 2021, found no significant change in body mass, BMI, body fat percentage, fat mass or fat-free mass with betaine [9]. A 2018 randomized trial in 23 untrained collegiate women over eight weeks of resistance training reported larger reductions in body fat percentage and fat mass with betaine, while lean mass and strength improved over time in both groups [26]. A 2014 narrative review by Cholewa and colleagues described possible benefits to performance and body composition with some conflicting findings and poorly understood mechanisms [25].

CrossFit and team-sport trials. A 2020 randomized trial by Moro and colleagues followed 29 CrossFit trainees for six weeks; the betaine group's back squat 3-rep max rose 3.23 percent (versus a non-significant 2.05 percent for placebo) with no significant between-group difference, and body composition, rowing and anaerobic test results did not change significantly [10]. A 2023 crossover trial of 43 CrossFit practitioners found an 8.7 percent improvement in a high-intensity workout and a 7.0 percent rise in testosterone with betaine at two doses over three weeks, and no change in Wingate power, body composition or cortisol [12]. In a 14-week randomized trial in 29 professional youth soccer players, betaine was associated with higher testosterone and testosterone-to-cortisol ratio but no significant group difference in lean mass or body fat, and a companion report found group-by-time interactions favouring betaine for VO2max, anaerobic peak power and strength [13][27]. A double-blind crossover study of 10 adolescent handball players reported more repetitions in leg and bench press with betaine and lower post-exercise cortisol [17].

A randomized trial of 18 men combining betaine with blood flow restriction training found no between-supplement difference in total repetitions, a higher IGF-1 change with betaine and no evidence of a synergy with blood flow restriction [28]. Registered trials include betaine with blood flow restriction (NCT05790070), exercise and gut permeability (NCT06392360) and firefighter thermoregulation (NCT06042270) [29][30][31].

Endurance. A 2025 randomized, double-blind crossover trial by Nieman and colleagues in 21 cyclists gave betaine for two weeks before a 60 km time trial. Times averaged 112.8 minutes with betaine and 114.2 with placebo (1.41 minutes faster, p = 0.042), with no differences in gut permeability or cortisol and large shifts in one-carbon metabolites during recovery [11].
Other conditions: registered trials in homocystinuria, peroxisome disorders, steatohepatitis and lipid metabolism [18][19][20][21][23].

Grokipedia reports low toxicity, a generally recognised as safe classification for food use, and rapid absorption with peak plasma levels within about an hour [2]. The sports trials above did not report serious adverse events, and the 2010 trial measured hydration markers, hematocrit and glucose without differences from placebo [16].

An observational literature links gut-microbe metabolism of choline-containing compounds to trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) and cardiovascular risk [32][33]; a trial examined TMAO in vegetarians [34]. These studies concern choline pathways and are not direct tests of betaine supplements.

Betaine donates a methyl group to convert homocysteine to methionine through betaine-homocysteine S-methyltransferase, and is an osmoprotectant that stabilises proteins and cell structures under osmotic stress [2][35][3]. Craig's 2004 review describes the osmolyte and methyl-donor roles and links low methyl-group supply to raised homocysteine and fatty liver [3].

Proposed performance mechanisms, discussed by Lee and colleagues, include effects on lactate and fatty-acid metabolism, cell volume defence, protection of citric-acid-cycle enzymes, support for creatine synthesis through methyl donation, phosphagen metabolism and neural factors; they considered osmoprotection an unlikely explanation because hydration was controlled [16]. Reports of higher testosterone and IGF-1 with betaine in some trials have been interpreted as anabolic signalling [12][13][28]. Betaine has also been studied in inflammation research [36] and in nutrition and epigenetics reviews [37].

Grokipedia describes rapid absorption with peak plasma levels within about an hour [2]. Trials of betaine for performance measure serum betaine and one-carbon metabolites such as dimethylglycine, sarcosine and methionine, which rose with supplementation in the 2025 cycling trial [11].

Betaine was first isolated in 1869 from sugar beet molasses by Hermann Scheibler, according to Grokipedia, which also dates the elucidation of its methyl-donor role to the 1940s and its osmoprotectant role in bacteria to the 1960s [2]; these dates come from an AI-generated source and were not independently verified. Wikipedia notes that glycine betaine was discovered in sugar beet in the nineteenth century and that historically the term was reserved for trimethylglycine [1].

Trials of betaine for exercise performance were published from the late 2000s onward, including a 2009 study by Hoffman and colleagues and the 2010 Connecticut trial, some funded by betaine manufacturers [16][25].

Betaine appears on T Nation almost entirely as an ingredient in the site's own pre-workouts and in training logs [4][5][15]. Betaine hydrochloride, sold for digestion, appears in separate threads; one poster said they were about to try betaine HCl with apple cider vinegar for a digestive problem [38]. Wikipedia notes that 'betaine' is a chemical class that includes cocamidopropyl betaine used in shampoos [1].

Craig publishes a review of betaine in human nutrition [3].

14-week randomized trials in youth soccer players report hormone and performance changes [13][27].
Meta-analysis of betaine and body composition reports no significant change [9].
